messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: cholesky factorization question
parts:
Hi all,

Following the manual, I have done some basic multi-normal fitting using cholesky factorization:

parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega_y;
  vector<lower=0>[K]      L_sigma_y;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[K,K] L_Sigma_Y;
  L_Sigma_Y <- diag_pre_multiply(L_sigma_y, L_Omega_y);
}

model {
  y   ~ multi_normal_cholesky (x, L_Sigma_Y);
  L_Omega_y ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1.5);
  L_sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 1);
}

I have 2 (relatively simple) questions:

1. for matrix L_SIgma_Y - should it be declared as matrix or chprodolesky_factor_cov?

2. If I want to recover the var-cov matrix, should I use tcrossprod (L_Sigma_Y) or multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose (L_Sigma_Y) or multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose?

Many thanks,

Andy

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: cholesky factorization question
parts: On Friday, November 20, 2015 at 5:01:50 AM UTC-5, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
I have 2 (relatively simple) questions:

1. for matrix L_SIgma_Y - should it be declared as matrix or cholesky_factor_cov?

It does not matter much. If declared in the transformed parameters block, the latter from will check that it is lower-triangular with positive diagonal entries, but those properties are satisfied by construction, so I tend to just declare it a matrix.
2. If I want to recover the var-cov matrix, should I use tcrossprod (L_Sigma_Y) or multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose (L_Sigma_Y) or multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose?

Again it does not matter much when declared in generated quantities (so autodiff is not relevant). The latter is faster because it does not multiply anything by zero, which saves a lot of memory allocations if the matrix is large and it has to autodiff.

Ben
